subject: Default priors for coefficients in logistic regression models

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Default priors for coefficients in logistic regression models
parts:
Hello all,

I noticed that Andrew mentioned in one of his posts on the development group, that 'We no longer recommend Cauchy as our first-choice default' in reference to logistic regression coefficients, I think (please correct me if wrong). So that I, and perhaps others, know for the translation of the regression examples in the BUGS books, etc. can I ask:

1. What do we currently recommend? Is there any reading on these specifically?

2. Is this true just for logistic regression or other more general models?


Best,

Ben

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Default priors for coefficients in logistic regression models
parts:
I’ve been doing N(0,1) as in our recent JEBS paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/stan_jebs_2.pdf
But Aki has said that he thinks student-t is better, maybe with 7 df?

And it’s not just for logistic regression, it’s for models more generally.  But logistic regression is particularly amenable to default priors because there’s a natural scale to the outcome, as (-5,5) corresponds to (.01, .99) on the probability scale.

Bob can now add this to our document on informative priors…

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Default priors for coefficients in logistic regression models
parts:
On Monday, August 3, 2015 at 11:20:41 AM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
1. What do we currently recommend? Is there any reading on these specifically?

A variety of things that may change from month to month. There are a lot of papers (perhaps not for the logistic regression case) that try to obtain priors that facilitate making a yes-no decision on whether the coefficient is zero, which is not particularly Bayesian and not a great goal (Rob McCullogh was going around this summer saying that "sparsity is part of your utility function not your prior density").

Outside of that, there are some papers whose goals are to prevent separation (mostly in the case of a binary outcome) and achieve regularization (for any regression model), which can be accomplished by a variety of prior distributions and don't prescribe a particular density or hyperparameter values. Approximately all of these papers specify independent priors on the coefficients that are also independent of the priors on any nuisance parameters, which doesn't make much substantive sense. We're going to go in a different direction for an R package of pre-compiled models, but we won't agree on the priors and thus have to offer different options to users that they don't want.
2. Is this true just for logistic regression or other more general models?

The separation thing is largely a concern for models with binary outcomes. The issues of regularization and how to specify a joint prior pertain to all regression models, but the answers depend on how the outcome is measured.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Default priors for coefficients in logistic regression models
parts:
Andrew's defaults are implcitly assuming that all predictors have
bene standardized, or even standardized to have std-dev = 0.5 rather
than std-dev = 1.

The higher-level recommendation is to use something that concentrates
mass around where you expect the value to be. Then there's the issue of
how much you want to admit outliers, ranging from Cauchy (Student-t, df=1),
through the one Andrew mentioned (Student-t, df=7), to normal (Student-t, df=infinity),
in decreasing order of tail fatness.

- Bob
